title: Lookahead and lookbehind
summary: Zero-width tests on the text around a match: (?=...), (?!...), (?<=...) and (?<!...), the backtracking trap in a negative lookahead, and extracting amounts after a currency code in C#.

steps.title: Look, but do not take
body: A **lookahead** `(?=...)` checks that some text comes next, without making it part of the match. It is
**zero-width**, like `^` or `\b`: it tests a position and consumes nothing.
| Pattern | Matches |
| `\w+\(` | `GetUser(`: the name **and** the bracket |
| `\w+(?=\()` | `GetUser`: a name that is followed by a bracket |
| `\w+(?!\()` | a word that is **not** followed by a bracket (careful, see later) |
Why it matters: the match is exactly the text you want to extract or replace, while the context only decides
**whether** it counts. No group to read, no bracket to trim afterwards.
Below, only names of methods being called are matched.

steps.prompt: A lookaround consumes nothing. What does this print?
steps.explain: The lookahead checks for `(` but leaves it out of the match. In the third line, `(?=p)` checks for `p` without moving, so `rice` must then match at that same `p`: it cannot, at any position.

steps.title: Release candidates
prompt: The build list mixes releases and release candidates: `3.5.1-rc 3.5.0 3.6.0-rc`. Find the version numbers that
are followed by `-rc`, **without** the `-rc` in the match: `3.5.1` and `3.6.0`.
hints: Match the version, then check for `-rc` with a lookahead.
steps.explain: Writing `-rc` without the lookahead would find the right builds but put `-rc` in every value.

steps.title: Negative lookahead, and the backtracking trap
body: `(?!...)` succeeds when the text does **not** come next. Try to find counts that are not durations with
`\d+(?!ms)`. On `150ms` it matches `15`!
Why: `\d+` first takes `150`, the lookahead sees `ms` and fails, so the engine **backtracks**: it gives back the
`0` and tries again. After `15` comes `0`, which is not `ms`, so the match succeeds. A negative lookahead only
tests one position; the quantifier before it can always move that position.
The fix is to forbid both ways out: not followed by another digit, and not by `ms`.
```text
Step through the broken version below and watch the engine give back the `0`.

steps.title: Counts, not durations
prompt: Find the numbers that are **not** durations. A duration is a number followed by `ms`, with or without one space
before the unit (`150ms`, `40 ms`). Do not return part of a duration either: `15` out of `150ms` is wrong.
hints: `[0-9]+(?! ?ms)` finds `15` and `4`. Forbid a following digit too.
steps.explain: Also refusing a following digit stops the engine from giving digits back. The leading `\b` stops it starting a match in the middle of a number.

steps.title: Lookbehind: what came before
body: `(?<=...)` checks the text **before** the current position, and `(?<!...)` checks that it is not there.
| Pattern | Matches |
| `(?<=\$)[0-9]+` | a number right after a dollar sign, without the `$` |
| `(?<!-)\$[0-9]+` | a dollar amount that is not preceded by a minus |
| `(?<=\bEUR ?)[0-9]+` | a number after `EUR`, with or without a space |
Not every engine allows every lookbehind. **.NET and JavaScript** (since ES2018) accept any pattern inside,
even `\s*`, so the last row works there. **Python's `re`** needs a fixed width and rejects it with
"look-behind requires fixed-width pattern". More on the other tools in the next lesson.
Below, only the dollar amounts are matched, without the sign.

steps.title: Dollar amounts without the sign
prompt: Extract dollar amounts **without** the `$`: whole dollars with optional cents (a dot and two digits). Other
numbers on the line are not amounts. Use a lookbehind.
hints: Start with `(?<=\$)`: the dollar sign must be escaped inside it too.
steps.explain: The `$` decides whether a number counts, but stays out of the value, so `decimal.Parse` can take the match as it is.

steps.prompt: Match each zero-width test to what it checks at the current position.
pairs: x does not come just before
a word starts or ends here
steps.explain: `=` means it must be there, `!` means it must not; `<` means look backwards. All four consume nothing, like `\b`.

steps.title: Charges, not refunds
prompt: In the payments log, refunds are written with a minus before the dollar sign: `-$12.50`. Find the **charges**:
a `$` amount with exactly two decimals, including the `$`, that is not preceded by `-`. Use a negative lookbehind.
steps.explain: The lookbehind sits right before the `$`. Here there is no backtracking trap: the `\$` must match at one exact place, so the engine cannot shift the start to dodge the minus.

steps.title: Amounts after a currency code
prompt: Finance exports invoices as free text: `EUR 12.50, USD 3, EUR40`. Write
`List<decimal> AmountsIn(string text, string currency)` that returns every amount that follows the given currency
code, in order. The code is a whole word in capitals, optionally followed by one space. Amounts are digits with
an optional dot and one or two decimals.
Use a **lookbehind** for the currency, so each match is the number alone, and build it from
`Regex.Escape(currency)` (the code comes from a config file). Parse with
template: var dojoText = "EUR 12.50, USD 3, EUR40, eur 7, XEUR 9";
Dojo.Eq("EUR amounts, with and without a space", new List<decimal> { 12.50m, 40m }, AmountsIn(dojoText, "EUR"));
Dojo.Eq("no amounts for GBP", new List<decimal>(), AmountsIn(dojoText, "GBP"));
Dojo.Eq("one decimal is fine", new List<decimal> { 0.5m, 1999m }, AmountsIn("fee EUR 0.5 then EUR 1999", "EUR"));
hints: The lookbehind is `(?<=\bEUR ?)` with the escaped code in place of `EUR`. .NET allows the optional space inside it.
